items.title: GoPro’s New MISSION 1 Cameras Just Got a Major Photography Upgrade
items.summary: One of the year's more unique and intriguing non-AI storylines has been GoPro’s further foray into cinema-camera-esque development with its new MISSION 1 series. While these new, compact, powerful, and affordable MISSION 1 series cameras may appeal most to filmmakers, action-adjacent videographers, and content creators, they’re also capable for photographers. And that’s where they just got a major improvement: the company released a free update that adds major enhancements to the series cameras’ photography capabilities, including zero-lag photo shutter response, continuous 50MP RAW photos, and support for anamorphic lenses. Here’s what you need to know. GoPro MISSION 1 Series Photography Update As the title suggests, this major update for the GoPro MISSION 1 series is focused almost entirely on photography. "For photographers, by photographers. That's how we approached updating the MISSION 1 Series photo experience. This update opens an exciting new chapter for photography on GoPro. Put a MISSION 1 Series camera in the Point-and-Shoot Grip and you have a seriously capable travel camera that's durable, mountable and can even shoot 8K video. It's the camera everyone from first-time buyers to seasoned photographers will want in their bag." - Jensen Granger, GoPro's Creative Director of Photography. The big highlight is the dramatically improved photo shutter response, which delivers hair-trigger sensitivity for more accurate photo capture. The company has also unveiled that holding the shutter button down will now capture continuous photos in rapid succession, which should be helpful for photogs for sure. Here’s a breakdown of all the new photography-focused updates for the MISSION 1 series: Rapid Photo: With the free firmware update, all MISSION 1 Series cameras will now feature zero-lag, ultra-responsive shutter button response that results in photos being captured the instant the shutter button is pressed. items.title: Are You a Panasonic LUMIX Shooter? Today’s a Good Day to Check for Firmware Updates
items.summary: As previously reported, Panasonic’s promised firmware updates for several popular LUMIX cameras are now available to download and install. Now, do you want to do so right away in all cases? Maybe not, since it's often wise to wait a few days, or weeks, before updating firmware in case new issues arise But if you want to go ahead, or if you’re simply curious about what new updates and features might be coming for some of your favorite cameras, here’s a full breakdown of the latest firmware updates for your Panasonic LUMIX cameras. Panasonic LUMIX Firmware Updates The big news is that four Panasonic LUMIX cameras are getting decent firmware updates that are, as always, free and available starting today. We covered the announcement of these firmware updates before and really focused on the S9 and its firmware 2.1 update being the most notable. And it still is, as the camera can now record 4K60p and Full HD 120p video in MP4 (Lite) format. The S9 is also set to get more Lens Fn options, and the updates upgrade support for the company’s latest LUMIX Flow versions. Here’s a full breakdown of the updates for all the cameras mentioned above. Panasonic LUMIX DC-S9 Addition of 4K 60p/50p and FHD 120p/100p/60p/50p recording options for MP4 (Lite). items.title: Film Quote of the Day: The Quietest Line About Blind Obedience in 'Pan's Labyrinth'
items.summary: I was a senior in high school when Guillermo del Toro’s 2006 masterpiece, Pan’s Labyrinth (El laberinto del fauno), came out. I remember going to the movies to see it, and having no idea I had to read subtitles. It took me a second to get used to them, but suddenly I was transported to a time and a place that both scared and awed me. Today, I want to go over one of the lines that stood out when I first read it, and how I keep returning to it when I think about the movie's totalitarian themes and its evil characters. Let's dive in. - YouTubewww.youtube.com The Scene in Question This is a movie set in 1944, when the Allies have invaded Nazi-held Europe. But in Spain, a troop of soldiers is sent to a remote forest to flush out the rebels who have been fighting a guerrilla war against them. These soldiers are led by Captain Vidal, a violent sadist who demands respect and order. He brings his new wife Carmen and her daughter from a previous marriage, 11-year-old Ofelia, with him. Carmen is pregnant, and he thinks the air out there is good for them. Ofelia witnesses her stepfather's sadistic brutality and is drawn into Pan's Labyrinth, a magical world of mythical beings, where she can escape the existence that is so harsh to her in the real world. Meanwhile, Captain Vidal attempts to root out the spies who would see him and his Franco regime members killed. In the scene we're talking about, Vidal has traced the spies back to Dr. Ferreiro, the local physician secretly treating the anti-fascist rebels. And he has to pay for his insolence. Before executing the doctor on the spot, Vidal demands to know why he disobeyed his direct orders. Dr. Ferreiro does not beg for his life. Instead, he says... “But Captain, to obey - just like that - for obedience's sake... without questioning... items.title: How a DP Shot a 2026 Horror Feature on a MiniDV Camcorder
items.summary: Cinematographer Ryan Thomas shot Casey Donahue's feature debut on two borrowed DVX100Bs. Panasonic's DVX100 line was the indie workhorse of the early 2000s, and the original model was the first small camcorder to record at a film-like 24 frames per second. The DVX100B was its last revision. It shoots standard definition to MiniDV tape. That makes it a strange pick for a feature premiering in 2026. Strange, and a lot of fun. In the film, Alice is heartbroken after a breakup, so she bargains with the devil for all the love in the world, then transforms into a siren-like figure who pulls men into her orbit before sliding into violent madness. Donahue funded it partly through Kickstarter, where 737 backers pledged $65,684 against a $50,000 goal. The film, My Love for You Is Deep but the Devil Loves Me Deeper, world premieres at Toronto After Dark, where it opens the festival's new Late Night Program at CineCycle, a slate built around more esoteric and experimental genre work. Doughboys Media and Devil Business produced, and the cast includes cameos from alt-comedy regulars James Urbaniak, Mike Mitchell, Kyle Mooney and Beck Bennett. If you came up on late-night cable thrillers, this one should feel familiar. We've written before about why a 20-year-old camcorder can be the right tool. Thomas tested in his living room, built a workflow with his colorist, and leaned into the noise and clipping a modern camera would hide. The old camera also helped the budget. There were no rentals, and the deep focus meant no AC was needed. We talked with Thomas ahead of the premiere about his kit, his tests, and what he's taking to his next shoot. items.title: Camera Operating for David Fincher—40 Takes and No Pans
items.summary: David Fincher is one of the most exacting directors working today, demanding hundreds of takes from his cast and crew to get a version of his vision that's as close to perfection as possible. His camera stays pretty fixed throughout this process, even when it's moving—meaning it doesn't drift or correct to get the right frame. Every movement, in characteristic Fincher style, is intentional and motivated. Peter Rosenfeld, SOC, has a unique perspective. He's operated The Social Network and Gone Girl for Fincher, along with American Sniper and Spider-Man: No Way Home. He breaks down the experience in a clip from CinePro's CineTalk podcast with host Hugo Will. The full episode is paywalled, but CinePro has shared some enticing clips. What this one about camera movement below. - YouTube www.youtube.com The Operator's Job Changes Every Movie Before getting to Fincher, Rosenfeld clears up a common misconception. Many people, Will included, assume direction flows neatly from director to DP to operator. Rosenfeld says it doesn't. "As a camera operator, you function as part of the three, right? There's the director, the cinematographer, and the camera operator. And your role changes on every single movie. Always different. Even if you're working with the same cinematographer, your role might be somewhat different on the next movie because the director is different." Sometimes the director hires the operator before the DP is even on board, he says. "And I've done many movies in my career where it's the director that hires me. I've done nine movies with Peyton Reed, you know, all the Marvel movies and stuff. And he hires me before the cinematographer is even hired. He calls you. So I have that relationship. So that's an entirely different thing. And each one of those movies was different because the cinematographer was changed. So the role that you fill is very political." items.summary: One of my buddies sold a horror spec for a few hundred thousand dollars last week and was shocked at the number. I mean, this year alone, we have Obsession crossing $500 million, Backrooms crossing $400 million, and Resident Evil crossing $300 million... and counting. The secret sauce of horror isn't just that it makes money; it's the sheer return on investment (ROI) studios see when they put a little money in and watch it explode. It's like buying gold over and over. Sure, there are bombs, but horror is a genre famous for the massive hits. The Blair Witch Project (1999): Produced for roughly $60,000; grossed over $248 million worldwide. Paranormal Activity (2007): Shot for $15,000 in a director’s home; pulled in $193 million. Get Out (2017): Budgeted at $4.5 million; grossed $255 million and earned four Oscar nominations.
